title: Stress, strain, and elastic response
objective: Relate tensile, shear, and bulk stress to deformation within a stated linear elastic regime and propagate measurement limits.
why: An instrument mount can satisfy every equilibrium equation and still deform enough to spoil a measurement. A longer wire and a thicker wire made from the same material respond differently to the same force. To predict those changes, connect internal force to stress, measured geometry to strain, and a material law to a stated range of validity. Then test what your measuring apparatus actually observes. This lesson develops those connections and the energy account they support.

prerequisites.label: Static equilibrium and support reactions
prerequisites.note: Isolate a body or one side of an internal cut. Equilibrium supplies force; compatibility supplies how connected parts deform.

prerequisites.label: Units, dimensions, and measurement evidence
prerequisites.note: Refresh squared and cubed prefixes, bounded uncertainty, and resolution before using small areas and displacements.

prerequisites.label: Work as an integral
prerequisites.note: Review force–displacement area and the difference between final force and average force during loading.

prerequisites.label: Energy accounts and model validity
prerequisites.note: Separate recoverable stored energy from dissipated energy and keep the reference configuration explicit.

prerequisites.label: Calculus I preparation
prerequisites.note: Preparation is under construction. The needed integrals are developed here for a linear force law and a polynomial axial-force distribution; this does not replace the academic calculus prerequisite.

sections.heading: Start with an internal cut, not the resultant
paragraphs: Consider a straight specimen pulled by two opposite end forces of magnitude $F$. Their external resultant can be zero while the specimen length changes. Cut the specimen across its axis and isolate one side. Equilibrium requires an internal axial force of magnitude $F$ across that cut, not $2F$ and not zero. The equal and opposite traction on the other cut face belongs to the other isolated body.

Use $L_0$ for original gauge length and $A_0$ for original cross-sectional area. Engineering normal stress is $\sigma=N/A_0$, with internal axial force $N$ positive in tension and negative in compression. Stress is force normalized by area; its SI unit is $\mathrm{Pa=N/m^2}$. Average stress need not equal the local stress near a hole, grip, abrupt area change, or concentrated load.

Engineering axial strain is $\epsilon=(L-L_0)/L_0=\delta/L_0$. It measures fractional change of length and has no unit of length. A strain of $0.0005$ is $0.05\%$ or $500$ microstrain, because one microstrain is $10^{-6}$ strain. The ratio $L/L_0$ is $1+\epsilon$, not the strain itself. An extension alone cannot compare differently sized specimens fairly.

Throughout this lesson, engineering quantities refer to the original geometry. True stress uses current area and logarithmic strain uses a different definition; neither is silently substituted here. The uniform small-strain approximation is stated for each model. Real load introduction, nonuniformity, temperature changes, preload, and time-dependent behavior require additional evidence.

sections.heading: Normalize units, then distinguish modulus from stiffness
paragraphs: Square or cube the entire unit conversion: $1\ \mathrm{mm^2}=10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2}$ and $1\ \mathrm{cm^3}=10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^3}$. Conveniently, $1\ \mathrm{N/mm^2}=1\ \mathrm{MPa}$ and $1\ \mathrm{GPa}=1000\ \mathrm{MPa}$. For a round specimen of diameter $d$, $A_0=\pi d^2/4$. Using diameter as radius introduces a factor of four before any material law is applied.

In a supplied uniaxial linear elastic regime, $\sigma=E\epsilon$ with positive Young modulus $E$. Both stress and modulus have pressure units. Combining the definitions gives $\delta=FL_0/(EA_0)$, so the specimen stiffness is $k=F/\delta=EA_0/L_0$ and its compliance is $C=1/k$. Compliance has displacement-per-force units. A modulus describes the assumed material response; a stiffness describes a particular specimen and loading geometry.

At fixed nonzero force, doubling area halves stress, strain, extension, and stored energy. Doubling length leaves stress and strain unchanged but doubles extension. At fixed end displacement, however, doubling area doubles the required force while strain and stress stay unchanged. Name the held variable before comparing two specimens. There is no universal rule that a geometry change always raises or lowers force or energy.

Signed compression gives negative stress, strain, and axial extension under the same local law. This does not establish that a slender compressed member remains straight: buckling is a separate instability. Compression examples here assume a short, laterally supported ideal specimen. Bending and buckling are excluded; a calculated axial stiffness is not a load rating.

sections.heading: Shear changes shape; hydrostatic pressure changes volume
paragraphs: For an ideal simple-shear element, let $A$ be the loaded face area, $h$ the perpendicular separation of the moving faces, and $\delta_x$ their relative tangential shift. Engineering shear strain is $\gamma=\delta_x/h=\tan\theta\approx\theta$ only for a small angle measured in radians. The constitutive law is $\tau=G\gamma$, where $\tau=F_t/A$ and $G>0$ is the shear modulus. Do not replace $h$ by the face width or use the area of a different face.

A homogeneous static shear element also needs complementary shear tractions on other faces to balance moments. A sketch of two opposite tangential forces alone is not a complete static free-body diagram of that element. This lesson supplies the full ideal shear state implicitly and calculates one face shift; it does not claim that an unconstrained isolated block can hold that state using an unbalanced couple.

Under a hydrostatic pressure increase $\Delta p>0$, the reference volume $V_0$ decreases. Define volumetric strain $\epsilon_V=\Delta V/V_0$ and bulk modulus by $\Delta p=-K\epsilon_V$ for the supplied small-strain linear model. Thus $\Delta V=-V_0\Delta p/K$ and compressibility is $\beta=1/K$ in $\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$. Equal pressure forces on different faces do not become one summed axial force: hydrostatic compression concerns a stress state, not a single net force.

The bulk reference is the state at baseline pressure; $\Delta p$ is its increment. Solids can resist both shape change and volume change. A simple equilibrium fluid has no static shear modulus even though its bulk modulus can be positive. Young, shear, and bulk moduli refer to different loading conditions; they are not interchangeable numbers.

sections.heading: Recoverable energy follows from a loading path
paragraphs: Start at an unstressed reference and increase force quasistatically within a reversible linear regime. Then $F=k\delta$ and $U=\int_0^\delta kq\,dq=k\delta^2/2=F\delta/2=F^2L_0/(2EA_0)$. The integration variable $q$ is a temporary displacement. The factor one half comes from the rising force, not an arbitrary correction. Using the final force over the entire displacement would overstate the work by a factor of two.

Divide by the reference volume to obtain energy density $u=\sigma^2/(2E)=\sigma\epsilon/2$. A pascal is also one joule per cubic meter. Signed compression still gives $U\ge0$ because both force and extension are negative, and the integral follows from zero to negative displacement. The positive energy is returned during reversible unloading. Net work around a closed admitted cycle is zero.

For simple shear, $u=\tau^2/(2G)$. For incremental hydrostatic compression, $U=-\int_0^{\Delta V}\Delta p(v)\,dv=(\Delta p)^2V_0/(2K)$, and $u=(\Delta p)^2/(2K)$. The minus sign makes compression work positive when $\Delta V<0$. This incremental account excludes work due to the pre-existing baseline pressure; do not mix those reference conventions.

Elastic means recoverable deformation; linear means a proportional constitutive relationship in the stated range. A material can be elastic without a straight stress–strain curve. If the supplied range is exceeded, its modulus alone does not determine actual strain, residual deformation, energy loss, or the unloading curve. An unsupported extrapolated line is not evidence about any of those quantities.

sections.heading: Connected members need compatibility as well as equilibrium
paragraphs: For axial members in series, a massless connection and no intermediate axial load give the same force in each member. Their extensions add, so $\delta=F\sum_iL_i/(E_iA_i)$ and $1/k_{\mathrm{eq}}=\sum_i1/k_i$. If an intermediate load or self-weight matters, the force need not be common. Every member must separately satisfy its constitutive range.

For members in parallel between rigid plates constrained to translate without rotation, assume no gaps or initial preload. Compatibility gives a common end displacement $\delta$. Equilibrium gives $F=\sum_iF_i=\delta\sum_i k_i$, hence $k_{\mathrm{eq}}=\sum_i k_i$ and $F_i=k_iF/k_{\mathrm{eq}}$. Equal displacement does not imply equal force when stiffnesses differ, or equal strain when lengths differ. If a plate can rotate, the displacement condition must be re-derived.

For nonuniform axial loading, take a short slice of length $dx$. Its extension is $d\delta=N(x)\,dx/[E(x)A(x)]$, so $\delta=\int N(x)/[E(x)A(x)]\,dx$. Its stored energy is $dU=N(x)^2dx/[2E(x)A(x)]$. These formulas require an axial small-strain model; they do not include shear deformation or bending merely because an integral is used.

For a vertical uniform bar of length $L$ carrying a bottom load $P$, measure $x$ upward from its lower end. A cut supports the bottom load and the weight below it, giving $N(x)=P+\rho A g x$. Integrating yields $\delta=PL/(EA)+\rho gL^2/(2E)$. Maximum normal stress is at the top, while average stress determines total extension for constant $EA$. Replacing the distribution by its maximum everywhere would overpredict extension.

sections.heading: Lateral response is conditional on the material model
paragraphs:
Under uniaxial stress, define Poisson ratio $
u=-\epsilon_{\perp}/\epsilon_{\parallel}$. Positive $
u$ means tensile axial extension accompanies lateral contraction; a negative value means lateral expansion and is possible in an auxetic material. The small fractional volume change is the sum of the three normal strains, so in this uniaxial case $\epsilon_V\approx(1-2
u)\sigma/E$. Products of small strains are omitted in that approximation.

For homogeneous isotropic small-strain linear elasticity only, $E=2G(1+
u)=3K(1-2
u)$. Positive finite $E,G,K$ imply $-1<
u<1/2$. These relations constrain an assumed isotropic model; they are not universal for wood, direction-dependent crystals, or composites. Giving one modulus without the additional isotropic information does not generally specify all other responses.

At $\nu=1/2$, incompressibility is a limiting model with zero first-order volume strain and unbounded bulk modulus, while $G=E/3$ remains finite. It is not valid to divide by zero and report a finite $K$. This extension connects axial measurements to volume response without requiring tensor notation; the optional MIT reading develops the more general energy formulation.

sections.heading: A displacement reading includes the apparatus
paragraphs: Suppose a device reports $d_{\mathrm{read}}=d_0+(C_{\mathrm{specimen}}+C_{\mathrm{fixture}})F$. The constant zero offset $d_0$ cancels in differences, so $C_{\mathrm{total}}=(d_2-d_1)/(F_2-F_1)$ for distinct forces. Subtract independently known fixture compliance before calculating $E=L_0/(A_0C_{\mathrm{specimen}})$. Fitting a straight line alone cannot distinguish the two compliances.

If fixture compliance is positive, ignoring it makes the specimen appear more compliant and underestimates its modulus. Zero offset, changing grip slip, temperature drift, and resolution are separate limitations. A constant-offset correction cannot repair a force-dependent grip error. The simulation uses exact prescribed inputs and has none of these measurement effects unless you introduce and label them in a calculation.

A nonzero force paired with a negative extension under the stated positive-modulus tensile model is inconsistent data or an inconsistent model, not evidence for a negative Young modulus. A zero-force, zero-extension pair cannot identify a modulus: many positive moduli satisfy it. To infer a parameter, the experiment must contain a nonzero signal and known geometry, load, and apparatus behavior.

For a displayed resolution step $h$ with rounding-to-nearest, a single reading has a rounding bound of $h/2$ under that specific rule. The difference of two independently rounded readings has a worst-case bound of $h$. These are allowed intervals, not standard deviations or confidence levels. If the allowed positive extension can approach zero, $E=FL/(A\delta)$ has no finite upper bound from those readings alone.

sections.heading: Propagate bounds before making a model claim
paragraphs: For positive independent allowed intervals in $F,L,A,E$, extension increases with $F,L$ and decreases with $A,E$. Therefore $\delta_{\min}=F_{\min}L_{\min}/(E_{\max}A_{\max})$ and $\delta_{\max}=F_{\max}L_{\max}/(E_{\min}A_{\min})$. The extremes assume those endpoint combinations are allowed jointly. Correlated measurements can rule out corners; uncertainty is not automatically independent just because it appears in four columns.

If area comes from a round diameter, use $A=\pi d^2/4$ at each endpoint. A first-order sensitivity estimate gives $d\delta/\delta\approx dF/F+dL/L-dE/E-2\,dd/d$. The factor two describes small relative changes; exact finite bounds use the squared endpoint diameters. Do not substitute an approximate symmetric percentage interval for an exact nonlinear interval without saying so.

A supplied tensile stress cap $\sigma_{\lim}$ and strain-magnitude cap $\epsilon_{\lim}$ jointly permit $|\sigma|\le\min(\sigma_{\lim},E\epsilon_{\lim})$. Under a uniform axial model the corresponding force cap is $A_0\min(\sigma_{\lim},E\epsilon_{\lim})$. Equality is admitted but limiting. An exceeded cap means this constitutive model no longer establishes the response; it does not, by itself, prove yielding or fracture.

The interactive loading stage is an ordered sequence, not physical elapsed time. After the first exceeded bound, unloading remains unknown even when the applied force re-enters the nominal range or reaches zero. The next lesson introduces additional plasticity and fracture evidence needed to make further statements. Do not replace missing evidence with an assumed return along the elastic line.

sections.heading: Carry out a reproducible simulation investigation
paragraphs: Use the investigation below to record predictions before revealing each result. Start with the axial baseline; compare double area at fixed force with double area at fixed extension. Then compare a longer specimen, signed compression, shear, and bulk compression. Keep an input table so each comparison changes a named condition rather than several unexplained variables.

At a supplied bound, inspect the exact event as well as the regular loading samples. Compare a peak exactly on the stress limit with a peak beyond it. Repeat with the strain limit active first. Record the known applied loading separately from any strain, energy, or shape that the model does not establish. The table is equivalent to the diagrams, and its region and stage slider support keyboard use.

Save at least six predicted and checked states, one independent unit conversion, one work integral, and a causal explanation for the two area comparisons in lesson notes. Include one apparatus or resolution limitation absent from the ideal simulation. The four-criterion rubric below the controls checks traceable units, calculations, controlled comparisons, and model limits; it is a proposed self-assessment rather than an official NU laboratory grade.

This investigation is entirely simulated. It assigns no home tensioning, breaking, suspended-load, or pressure experiment. Real elastic testing can store and suddenly release energy and needs suitable equipment, restraints, procedures, and supervision. No official equipment requirement has been established for this platform activity. The numerical material properties here are hypothetical and do not identify a safe real specimen.

examples.title: One force, three ways to check the axial result
examples.prompt: A hypothetical specimen has L0=2 m, A0=4 mm², E=100 GPa, and a tensile force of 200 N. Its supplied stress and strain limits are 100 MPa and 0.002. Find stress, strain, extension, stiffness, and energy; check the range first.

steps.reason: N/mm² equals MPa. One internal force acts across the cut; the opposite end force is not added to it.
Both bounds hold. The strain is 500 microstrain, not 0.0005 meters.
Recover the gauge length from δ/ε as an independent geometry check.
The reference volume is 8×10^-6 m³, so energy density times volume gives the same 0.1 J.

examples.conclusion: The admitted response is 50 MPa, 0.0005 strain, 1 mm extension, 200 kN/m stiffness, and 0.1 J stored energy.

examples.title: Signed compression stores positive energy
examples.prompt: Use a short, laterally supported ideal specimen with L0=0.5 m, A0=3 mm², E=80 GPa, and F=−120 N. Assume its supplied reversible range includes this state; buckling is excluded.

steps.reason: Compression is negative with the stated normal-stress convention.
The specimen shortens, but its positive stiffness remains a property of the assumed geometry and material.
The integral runs toward negative displacement with negative force. Their product is positive; recoverable energy is not signed like extension.

examples.conclusion: Negative extension does not imply negative stored energy or establish stability against buckling.

examples.title: Use diameter once, and keep pi exact
examples.prompt: A circular specimen has diameter 2 mm, length 1 m, E=100 GPa, and force $80\pi$ N. The supplied linear range admits the loading.

steps.reason: Radius is 1 mm. Pi cancels from stress but remains in the specimen's area.
Pressure units match before dividing. Extension is obtained from strain times the original length.
The exact coefficient of pi belongs to stiffness and energy; it is not an angle conversion.

examples.conclusion: Area is $\pi\ \mathrm{mm^2}$, extension is 0.8 mm, and energy is $4\pi/125$ J. Treating diameter as radius would quadruple the area.

examples.title: The held condition changes the area comparison
examples.prompt: Start from the 200 N, 2 m, 4 mm², 100 GPa baseline. Double the area to 8 mm². Compare holding force at 200 N with holding extension at 1 mm.

steps.reason: Area doubles stiffness for fixed length and material.
At fixed force, the increased stiffness halves displacement and energy.
At fixed displacement, force and energy double. Strain stays 0.0005, so stress stays 50 MPa.

examples.conclusion: A geometry comparison is incomplete until its load or displacement control is named.

examples.title: Find the shear shift and its energy
examples.prompt: A hypothetical small-shear element has loaded face area 60 mm², face separation h=0.02 m, G=0.8 GPa, and signed tangential force 120 N. The supplied full shear state admits this loading.

steps.reason: Use the area of the loaded face and the shear modulus, not Young modulus.
The shift is relative between faces. The small angle is approximately 0.0025 radians, not degrees.
Check using half the tangential force times the shift: 120×0.00005/2=0.003 J.

examples.conclusion: Engineering shear strain is 0.0025 and face shift is 50 μm. Complementary shear tractions are part of the assumed static model.

examples.title: Bulk compression needs a minus sign
examples.prompt: A reference volume of 500 cm³ has K=2 GPa. Apply a hydrostatic pressure increase of 4 MPa within its supplied range. Calculate volume change, final volume, compressibility, and incremental stored energy.

steps.reason: Positive pressure increase reduces volume.
Compressibility is the reciprocal of bulk modulus, not the fractional volume change in this particular trial.
Convert cm³ to m³ for pressure-volume work. The pressure increment grows from zero, so its mean is half the final increment.

examples.conclusion: The final volume is 499 cm³ and incremental stored energy is 2 J. Baseline-pressure work is outside this reference account.

examples.title: Series members share force, not extension
examples.prompt: Two unstressed members are joined axially in series with a massless unloaded connection. Member 1: L1=1 m, A1=2 mm², E1=100 GPa. Member 2: L2=0.5 m, A2=1 mm², E2=50 GPa. A 100 N tensile load is admitted in both members.

steps.reason: With force in N, length in m, E in GPa and area in mm², these numerical expressions return mm. Confirm by converting one term entirely to SI.
Compatibility adds extensions; it does not make them equal.
The second member has twice the stress and four times the strain. Separate range checks would be needed if limits were supplied.

examples.conclusion: Equal force can produce unequal stresses, strains, and extensions. The equivalent stiffness is less than either member stiffness.

examples.title: Parallel compatibility resolves the load split
examples.prompt: Two unstressed 1 m members connect rigid plates constrained to translate without rotation. E1=100 GPa, A1=2 mm²; E2=50 GPa, A2=6 mm². The total tensile load is 250 N and both responses remain admitted.

steps.reason: Equilibrium alone gives only F1+F2=250. Common plate displacement supplies the missing relation.
The second member has the larger area and lower modulus but larger total stiffness. It carries more force while having less stress.
Sum the two individual energies as a check. These plates do not rotate, and there are no initial gaps or preloads.

examples.conclusion: The load split is 100 N and 150 N at a common 0.5 mm extension; an equal-force split would violate compatibility.

examples.title: A hanging bar has a stress gradient
examples.prompt: A uniform hypothetical hanging bar has L=2 m, A=10 mm², E=100 GPa, density 5000 kg/m³, g=10 m/s², and an additional bottom load P=100 N. The entire supplied axial range is admitted. Measure x upward from the bottom.

steps.reason: A cut supports the bottom load plus the weight of the length x below it.
EA is 10^6 N. The integral gives 201 N m; the top force is 101 N, while the mean force is 100.5 N.
Squaring the force before integration gives 20200+2/3 N² m. Half the bottom load times the total extension alone omits the work of the distributed weight.

examples.conclusion: Maximum stress is 10.1 MPa and total extension is 0.201 mm. Distributed loading requires a local force and energy account.

examples.title: Check a conditional isotropic model
examples.prompt: A hypothetical homogeneous isotropic material has E=120 GPa, Poisson ratio 0.25, and uniaxial tensile stress 60 MPa. Find shear and bulk moduli and the first-order strains.

steps.reason: These conversions use the stated isotropic small-strain model; E alone would not be enough.
There are two equal transverse strains in this uniaxial isotropic case.
The sum omits products of strains. It is a small-strain volume approximation, not the exact finite product of three stretch ratios.

examples.conclusion: The first-order volume increase is 0.00025. This uniaxial loading is not the same stress state as hydrostatic pressure.

examples.title: Separate fixture compliance from material modulus
examples.prompt: A synthetic apparatus reports 0.3, 0.9, and 1.5 mm at 0, 100, and 200 N. The specimen has L0=2 m and A0=4 mm²; independently supplied fixture compliance is 0.001 mm/N. Assume an admitted linear specimen and constant offset.

steps.reason: The slope uses differences to cancel the constant offset. The zero-force reading confirms the intercept.
The specimen extension at 200 N is 1 mm. The other 0.2 mm of load-dependent extension is in the fixture.

Ignoring fixture compliance understates E. If two displacement readings each round to a 0.1 mm step, their difference can err by up to 0.1 mm from rounding alone, which is 10% of this specimen signal.

examples.conclusion: An apparently straight apparatus response does not prove its slope is the specimen compliance. The resolution statement is a bound under a rounding rule, not a statistical uncertainty.

examples.title: Compute finite uncertainty bounds without invented probabilities
examples.prompt: Treat all endpoint combinations as allowed: F∈[198,202] N, L∈[1.99,2.01] m, A∈[3.9,4.1] mm², E∈[98,102] GPa. The model admits this whole range. Bound extension and maximum tensile stress.

steps.reason: The numerator increases extension; the denominator decreases it. Select opposite denominator endpoints for the minimum and maximum.
The stress bound needs only force and area. The modulus uncertainty does not directly change F/A.
If all other inputs are exact and area comes from diameter, the exact extension interval is nonlinear and asymmetric. A roughly ±2% estimate is only first order.

examples.conclusion: The extension is bounded by about 0.94218 and 1.06232 mm. No probability or confidence level follows from the supplied allowed intervals.

examples.title: Exceeding the range leaves unloading unknown
examples.prompt: Use the axial baseline L0=2 m, A0=4 mm², E=100 GPa. The stress cap is 100 MPa and strain cap is 0.002. Prescribe a force path 0→500→0 N. Loading stage runs 0→1 to the peak and 1→2 back to zero.

steps.reason: The stress cap is tighter than the strain cap; both must be checked.
These are the last admitted loading values. The loading-stage boundary is 400/500=0.8.

The peak force is known but peak extension, energy, and later unloading are not established by the supplied law. At stage 1.2 the force returns to 400 N, but the earlier unsupported excursion remains part of its history.
A different trial whose peak is exactly 400 N stays inside the supplied reversible model and returns to zero strain and energy. This statement cannot be transferred to the 500 N trial.

examples.conclusion: A known final force of zero is insufficient to infer zero permanent set after a range excursion. A new constitutive history or observations are required.

guided.title: Check both limits before reporting extension
guided.setup: A hypothetical axial specimen has L0=1 m, A0=2 mm², E=100 GPa, and an applied tensile load of 300 N. Its supplied linear law admits stress magnitudes up to 100 MPa and strains up to 0.002. Identify the demanded stress and the last admitted tensile force and extension, then decide whether the actual extension at 300 N follows from the supplied law.
before: Use one 300 N internal axial force and the original 2 mm² section. Whole-body balance does not make internal loading zero.
Express E in MPa. Convert the strain bound into a stress bound and intersect it with the separate 100 MPa cap.
Calculate limiting force and limiting extension at the last admitted state. Keep those distinct from the actual response at the requested 300 N.

question.prompt: Calculate the signed stress demand, effective admitted stress cap, largest admitted tensile force, and extension at that limiting force. Then choose what can be established about the actual extension at 300 N.

fields.label: Demanded tensile stress
fields.help: Enter an exact value or equivalent fraction in the labeled unit.

fields.label: Effective admitted stress cap
fields.help: Enter an exact value or equivalent fraction in the labeled unit.

fields.label: Largest admitted tensile force
fields.help: Enter an exact value or equivalent fraction in the labeled unit.

fields.label: Extension at the admitted force limit
fields.help: Enter an exact value or equivalent fraction in the labeled unit.

options.label: Actual extension is not established because the stress cap is exceeded
options.feedback: The 150 MPa demand exceeds the 100 MPa cap. The supplied law establishes the 200 N limiting state, but does not establish extension at 300 N.

options.label: Extension is 1.5 mm because the extrapolated strain is below 0.002
options.feedback: The formal strain 0.0015 passes one bound, but the 150 MPa stress demand fails the separate 100 MPa cap. Both conditions must hold before that deformation is established.

options.label: Use both end forces and report 3 mm from a 600 N load
options.feedback: A cut through the specimen balances one side with 300 N. Adding opposite end-force magnitudes double-counts the internal force; it also fails the range check.

options.label: Extension is established because 150 MPa is far below the 100 GPa modulus
options.feedback: Young modulus is the stress–strain slope, not a strength or proportional-limit rating. Compare stress with the separately supplied cap.

hints: N/mm² equals MPa, so the demanded stress is 300/2. Do not add the opposite end force.
E=100000 MPa makes the strain-bound stress 200 MPa. Intersect it with the independent 100 MPa cap.
At the effective cap, F=Aσ and δ=(σ/E)L. These describe the last admitted state, not the unsupported requested peak.
explanation: $\sigma=300/2=150\ \mathrm{MPa}$ — One internal force and original area give the stress demand.
$\sigma_{\lim}=\min(100,100000(0.002))=100\ \mathrm{MPa}$ — The stress cap is more restrictive than the strain cap.
$F_{\lim}=2(100)=200\ \mathrm N,\quad\delta_{\lim}=(100/100000)(1)=0.001\ \mathrm m=1\ \mathrm{mm}$ — Compute deformation at the admitted boundary.

Hooke's law would formally extrapolate 1.5 mm at 300 N, but the stress range has already been exceeded. That number is not an established actual response, and exceeding the model does not by itself establish fracture.
question.answerSummary: Stress demand 150 MPa; effective cap 100 MPa; limiting tensile force 200 N; limiting extension 1 mm. Actual extension at 300 N is not established.

guided.after: In the investigation, load Strain limit first and explain why the active condition changes. Save one incorrect prediction and its correction. If you used a modulus as a strength rating, review the distinction between a constitutive slope and its validated range.

interaction.prompt: Predict stress and the admitted range before predicting deformation. Compare material response with specimen geometry, integrate the reversible load path, and identify exactly where the supplied elastic model stops establishing strain and energy.

summary: Stress is internal force per original area; strain is deformation normalized by reference geometry. $1\ \mathrm{MPa}=1\ \mathrm{N/mm^2}$.
For the supplied axial model, $\sigma=E\epsilon$, $\delta=FL/(EA)$, and $k=EA/L$. Material modulus and specimen stiffness have different meanings and units.
Shear uses $\tau=G\gamma$ with face shift over face separation. Bulk compression uses $\Delta V/V_0=-\Delta p/K$.
Integrating a reversible linear load gives $U=F\delta/2$. Compression can have negative force and displacement while energy stays nonnegative.
Series compatibility adds extensions at common force. Translation-only parallel plates impose common displacement and stiffness-dependent load sharing.
Measure the specimen signal separately from offset, fixture compliance, and resolution. Allowed finite bounds do not imply a probability distribution.
Check every supplied validity bound and the prior loading history before reporting deformation. A return to zero load after an unsupported excursion does not prove elastic recovery.
retrieval: Tomorrow, derive the axial extension and energy from the stress and strain definitions without looking up the formulas. Explain why double area has opposite energy effects under fixed force and fixed extension. A week later, solve a new shear, bulk, and range-check form. Review Units, dimensions, and measurement evidence for squared prefixes or uncertainty errors; review Work as an integral for a missing factor one half; use the next lesson for residual deformation and fracture evidence.
